title: Capacity census smoke test notes
content:
Goal: quick smoke run to census token-level latency and throughput behaviour when we step traffic from 0 -> target QPS. Primary objective was to catch major tail modes and verify warm-cache priming benefit at small scale before running full cluster sweep.

Experimental setup:
- Model: rw-open-13b-8k-quantized (cpu/gpu split on host), 1 shard per GPU.
- Hardware: 4 x A100-equivalent nodes (dedicated pool) for the smoke run.
- Runtime flags: batching.on=true, kv_cache.enabled=true, batch_timeout_ms=6, max_batch_tokens=4096
- Workload: synthetic client that replays traces sampled from last-week production (mix of short 16-token queries (60%), medium 128-token (30%), long 512-token (10%)).
- Arrival pattern: stepped Poisson -> hold at each step for 120s (30, 60, 120, 240 QPS).
- Two cache states: cold (node restart, cache empty) and warm (run a 5-minute priming replay at 50 QPS with same trace mix).

Key runs and raw observations: (numbers are aggregated across the 120s hold window for each step; sample size ~11k requests at 240QPS)

Step | State | p50 (ms) | p95 (ms) | p99 (ms) | peak QPS observed
-----|-------|----------|----------|----------|------------------
30   | cold  | 28       | 85       | 220      | 30               
30   | warm  | 26       | 42       | 78       | 30               
60   | cold  | 35       | 110      | 480      | 60               
60   | warm  | 29       | 55       | 110      | 60               
120  | cold  | 48       | 210      | 1.4k     | 118              
120  | warm  | 34       | 88       | 210      | 120              
240  | cold  | 72       | 520      | 3.7k     | 190 (queueing)
240  | warm  | 48       | 170      | 800      | 238              

Interpretation / notes:
- Warm priming buys a lot of tail reduction (p99 down ~4-5x at mid steps). Effects are most pronounced for the medium/long queries where KV reuse matters.
- Cold runs at higher steps show clear queuing/backpressure: peakQPS observed << target (e.g., 190 vs 240) and p99 explodes beyond 3s. This indicates our autoscaler/queueing threshold kicks in too late or the per-node concurrency cap is too conservative for this workload.
- The p95 surge on cold starts appears to be correlated with kernel wake-up and CUDA context thrash on this particular node flavor; we saw long tails only on ~2% of requests which aligns with GPU preemption events in kernel logs. Need to confirm with /var/log/nvidia and kube events.
- Batch timeout of 6ms seems reasonable for steady-state but contributes to larger batches (and thus longer single-request latencies) during the high-step cold runs. Might reduce to 3-4ms for aggressive latency SLOs.

Quick actionable hypotheses:
1) Add a short prefill pass (5–10s at 20–30% of target QPS) after node start to pre-warm KV cache and kernels. Should reduce the cold p99 spike.
2) Re-evaluate node-level concurrency cap: increasing in small increments may allow the cluster to reach target QPS without queueing. Must guard for head-of-line blocking.
3) Introduce a soft-priority fast lane for short queries (<=32 tokens) to keep p50/p95 low even when bigger queries create longer batches.
4) Instrument kernel wake events and correlate with request traces (add a trace id tag to GPU driver logs).

Failures / anomalies captured:
- At 240 QPS cold run, one node emitted repeated "CUDA context timeout" messages (kube evict logs show restart at t+45s). Cause unclear — maybe driver bug + long-running kernel due to an outlier 2k-token request in the trace. Need reproduction with a controlled 2k token single request.
- Observed small set (~0.3%) of requests with negative client RTT (clock skew) — ignore for now but note for upstream trace aggregation.

Next steps / experiments to run:
- Re-run the 240 QPS cold step with: batch_timeout_ms=4, concurrency_cap +10% on nodes, and a dedicated 30s prefill at 40 QPS. Compare p99.
- Run the same sweep but replace the longest 10% of queries with a capped 512-token set to see tail sensitivity.
- Capture GPU driver traces (nvidia-smi dmon + kernel ring buffer) during the next cold high-step to correlate.

Housekeeping: captured logs in the run directory: s3://redwood-perf/census/2024-11-12/theo-smoke-run-01/ (configs, raw traces, pod logs). Jira ticket created (INF-4821) for follow-ups and driver-level investigation.

Notes to self: keep these smoke runs short and focused — they catch big failure modes quickly. For full census we'll need similar runs across at least 3 node flavors (A100, T4-equivalent, and older V100-equivalent) and the dedicated cluster autoscaler config space.
